items.body:
Skewed dub specialist label Blundar host a mutant cumbia dub haunting by Bogotá’s ezmeralda, a leading figure of wayward ambient shook up from the Latin American bush of ghosts...

Preceded by an LP for Tra Tra Trax’s Ambie-Tón divison, and an EP with Éter Editions, ezmeralda continues to stake out a unique sort of tresillo metaphysics perhaps familiar to fans of Debit’s Modern Love albums or Elijah Minnelli fancies, or even The Caretaker’s slant on dusty ballroom standards, but applied to traditional cumbia. Everything inside is slowed and diffused to a vaporous crawl; bone-rubbed rhythms and basslines smudged into oblivion, and air hashed with spectral traces of flutes and accordions; ancient cries heard thru a modern lens.

For 16 minutes ezmeralda suspends perceptions of time and space with a sublime, deferred gratification, never quite fully revealing the forms, operating by suggestion in finely extracted and layered arrangements. The A-side feels as though we’re shored-up on some Mangrove-covered Caribbean coastline of Colombia at night, threats lurking below the briny surface and thick in the air, before the B-side brings the phantoms forward in what feels like Pole processing Elijah Minnelli’s anachronistic cumbia blooz...
items._genre: cumbia dub / ambient / experimental / world fusion
items._cn_summary: 波哥大音乐人ezmeralda在Blundar厂牌发行的这张专辑将传统cumbia节奏大幅减速与弥散化处理，形成一种接近蒸气状态的缓慢爬行质感。骨击节奏与低音线条被涂抹至模糊边缘，长笛与手风琴的频谱残影悬浮于空气之中，传统的哭喊声透过现代滤镜重新浮现。整张专辑仅十六分钟，却以暗示性的层叠编曲持续悬置听者对时空的感知，A面营造加勒比海岸夜间红树林覆盖的阴郁氛围，威胁潜伏于水面与空气之中，B面则将幽灵般的元素推至前景，呈现出一种类似Pole处理手法下的时代错位cumbia忧郁。评论将其与Debit、Elijah Minnelli、The Caretaker的实验美学相提并论，展示了拉丁美洲传统音乐在当代实验语境中的独特转化路径。

items.body:
Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run.

‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. However archänlèy, it’s still not even the best version - that honour is reserved to the 2.5hr digital-only ‘Quaristice.Quadrange.ep.ae’ brimming with extended versions, including an hour long mix of ‘Perlance subrange 6-36’ and deadly 10’ mix of ‘Tkakanren’ - but suffice it to say we’re made up to see this one in the wild on vinyl, at least.

The follow-up to a pivotal standout, 2004’s ‘Untilted’ (also reissued this year), ‘Quaristice’ really felt like a future upgrade to the system on its release in 2008. Completely unconcerned with prevailing or emerging trends of dubstep or UKF at the time, it sees the duo follow their noses for hardware/ software jams into the proper mutant body music, milling limbs to the meanest 112BPM electro swag in the twin-rotor electro hip hop gnash of ‘Tankakern’, and utterly wrecking the senses in the blizzard dynamic of ‘Fol3’, or manipulating sinew with deviant liquid B-Boy tekkerz on ’90101-5l-l’ - each of which feature in even better versions on the 2nd disc (and frankly better yet in their alternative extensions of the digi-only version). 

There are flashes of the melodic and harmonically curious Autechre we all know and love in opener ‘Altibzz’ (their love note to the magic of Altrincham), the aerated strings of ‘Theswere’, and almost Lynchian noir of ‘Notwo’, yet the whole thing feels to trigger muscle memories and flashbacks to club physicality, as felt in the corresponding live show at Pure in Manchester at the time. The mad thing is, as judged from recent live show, they still sound as rudely uncompromising and propulsive now, 17 years later, perhaps more than ever
items._genre: IDM / experimental electronic / electro / abstract hip-hop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Autechre第九张录音室作品，记录了二人组从硬件/软件即兴jam中提炼出的混合体：将112 BPM的锋利electro节奏与液态B-Boy技巧并置，使用合成器线条切割频谱空间，在密集颗粒与空灵弦乐之间反复切换。开篇'Altibzz'呈现旋律性命题，'Fol3'则以暴风雪般的动态摧毁听感，整体触发俱乐部身体的肌肉记忆。正文中特意提及另有2.5小时数字扩展版，包含长达一小时的混音与十分钟版本，说明核心素材在被压缩之前还有更极端的形态。此版本的重发使其首次以黑胶形式流通，对长期追踪这对组合硬件jam美学的听众而言，是将系统未来升级至可见形态的一次机会。

items.body: My daughter and I walked up Seventh Avenue on a balmy, post-thunderstorm July night to one of the most well-known, and most sacred, of all jazz venues on the planet, the storied Village Vanguard, to catch the opening night of a week-long residence by the trio Paradoxical Frog. Readers of the Free Jazz Blog might care to know this was a historical occasion and one that involved the reuniting of three musicians often discussed here at the FJC: pianist Kris Davis, saxophonist Ingrid Laubrock, and drummer Tyshawn Sorey. Behind the famous red doors that evening would perform an avant-garde trio that had not played together in over a decade. And the band’s unconventional leanings are perhaps less alien to the Vanguard than one might first guess. Davis and Sorey have performed at the Vanguard countless times, and Laubrock’s appearance is as rare and welcome as the recent celebrated stint of the James Brandon Lewis Quartet in the West Village club. This is to say nothing of the audience in the house that night: I spotted Sylvie Courvoisier a few seats behind me, and encountered William Parker outside the doors after the first set had concluded. Davis actually opened the show fact-checking the record. “I was corrected on social media,” she said. “It has not been fifteen years since the three of us played together; it has been eleven.” In any case, for listeners to either of the group’s two Cleanfeed recordings, 2010’s Paradoxical Frog , and 2012’s Union , it had been a long wait to hear these three masters perform in this distinct context. The opening night’s set consisted of four long compositions, all of which have appeared on record at some point. The first performance, a combination of Laubrock’s “Masterisk” and Davis’s “Union” spanned over twenty-nine minutes. Seeing the work live allowed me to confirm just how through-composed these Paradoxical Frog pieces are. Note the extensive paper scores in Davis’s and Sorey’s hands and the extensions on Laubrock’s music stand: a necessary tool to display the lengthy writings of each work without requiring the saxophonist to flip pages of these surprising compositions that challenge functional harmony and defy circular rhythm. The third work was “Whistlings” from 2020’s Blood Moon , the Intakt Records duo of Davis and Laubrock. The live performance, over twice the length of the original recording, featured Laubrock on soprano saxophone and Tyshawn Sorey on a sonic array of material, at times the room so quiet that Sorey’s percussion would consist of simply waving his brushes in the air, an effect that hauntingly filled the room with audible whisperings. The set concluded with Sorey’s “Slow Burn,” clocking in at over sixteen minutes and featuring the mysterious repetition of single notes on Davis’s piano keys. It was moving to see these three unite again, and I am certain I do not speak alone in voicing my hopes for more work in the future, maybe even a Live at the Village Vanguard recording to place among some of the mythical voices who have passed through that hallowed underground room. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / free improvisation / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于Paradoxical Frog三重奏在Village Vanguard开幕夜演出现场的乐评。评论详细记录了钢琴家Kris Davis、萨克斯演奏家Ingrid Laubrock和鼓手Tyshawn Sorey时隔十一年再度同台的历史性时刻。整场演出由四首长篇作品构成，其中Laubrock的"Masterisk"与Davis的"Union"融合演奏超过二十九分钟，展现出高度通过谱面构建的作曲逻辑。Davis与Sorey手持大量纸质乐谱，Laubrock的音乐架上也有延伸谱架，这种设置凸显了作品对功能和声与循环节奏的颠覆。第三首"Whistlings"选自Davis与Laubrock的Intakt厂牌专辑，演出时长为录音版的两倍以上，Sorey以刷子在空中划动制造出幽灵般的细碎声响。最后一首Sorey创作的"Slow Burn"时长逾十六分钟，钢琴反复敲击单音形成神秘循环效果。文章末尾作者呼吁能有更多后续合作乃至现场录音出版。

items.body: Geology and music often operate in symmetry; we tend to write of “sedimentary layers of sound” and “geological shifts.” In January, we reviewed Paleo Soul, a rock album by Washington geologist Barry Walker Jr. This month, we turn to Scottish musician Intertoto, who references the pioneering work of James Hutton while creating electronic pieces that imitate their corresponding landscapes. The key to both the geography and the music is change, though for obvious reasons the music shifts much swifter than its subjects. “Raw Lunar Concrete” opens the set in sedate fashion, referencing theories about materials that might allow construction on the moon. This immediate sci-fi angle tips the listener into speculative thinking: not just the history of the land, but its possible future. The album takes off with “Condor Launch,” inspired by the RM Condor Marine Base in East Argus, home to numerous squadrons since its opening in 1940. Suddenly, Siccar Point becomes a techno album, but the artist won’t remain there for long. After the appealing club vibe of “Cloud Chamber,” which shifts to the adjacent field of particle physics, the variety of timbres begins to increase, preceded by that track’s gradual recession. “Fold” features LabLab and dives into dub, as if mining the boulders and discovering previously hidden minerals. “Metallic Veins” is calmer, imitating the imperceptible shifts of metamorphosis with tiny rivers of electronic sound. In one sense, the track is the opposite of “Condor Launch;” in another, it uses the same elements, but slowed, thinned, rearranged. This and “Redox Dub” are the most intriguing cuts of the set, despite being the least immediate; to listen is to experience a sense of discovery. The closing “Foraber,” based on Hutton’s eureka moment at Siccar Point, splits the difference between ambient and electronic, lacking only the drums that would make it a club cut. The addition and subtraction of elements throughout the set is its greatest asset, highlighting the impact of slow, incremental change. (Richard Allen)
items._cn_summary: 苏格兰音乐人Intertoto以地质学家詹姆斯·赫顿的开创性理论为灵感，将电子声响对应苏格兰Siccar Point地区的地貌演变。专辑以月球建造材料的推测开场，随即转入受二战海军基地启发的techno段落，随后在dub与粒子物理学主题之间穿梭。曲目之间的元素增减与速度变化构成专辑核心手法，慢速、稀薄、重新排列的电子音流模拟变质作用的不可察觉位移。评论特别指出两首dub风格曲目虽不立即抓耳，却带来探索般的聆听体验，结尾曲目在ambient与电子之间取得平衡。整体呈现地质学与电子音乐的深层对称关系，强调缓慢渐进变化的力量。

items.body:
Sunn O))) guest players and Ideologic Organ mainstays Jessika Kenney and Eyvind Kang return with six new pieces for voice, viola, setar and electronics.

Recorded in Istanbul, Seattle and Bologna, The Face Of The Earth is more obviously Eastern in tone to the duo's last IO offering, Aestuarium. Taking its cue from classical Persian and Javanese traditions, and themed around the idea of "drawing the binary from the unary, like reflections from a mirror, and its inverse, the concealed identity", it's a collection of sonic riddles whose meaning can be unlocked, at least to some extent, by the "reading cards" provided in the insert. Despite the arcane mysticism at work, it's music of self-evident and ravishing beauty: from the medievalist balladry of 'Tavaf', to the pensive but restlessly percussive 'Kidung', Kenney's vocal performances are show-stopping throughout, and Kang's strings resonate powerfully around them. Over its short duration, the sparse voice and viola interplay of 'Ordered Pairs II' take on the character of spiritual jazz, while the looping and phasing techniques applied on 'Mirror Stage' come over like a courtly response to Steve Reich's 'It's Gonna Rain', and 'The Face Of The Earth' feels like the logical extension of the more avant-garde moments on Julia Holter's Ekstasis. Tremendous stuff.
items._genre: experimental / contemporary classical / world fusion / avant-garde vocal
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由曾参与Sunn O)))的歌手Jessika Kenney与中提琴家/塞塔琴演奏者Eyvind Kang合作，呈现六首为人声、中提琴、塞塔琴与电子设备而作的新作。录制跨越伊斯坦布尔、西雅图与博洛尼亚三地，灵感取自古典波斯与爪哇传统音乐，围绕从一元中映照出二元及其隐匿反转的哲学主题展开。专辑将仪式性的声乐与器乐置于稀疏的电子框架中：'Tavaf'呈现中世纪式的叙事谣曲质感，'Kidung'以思考性的人声配合连绵不绝的打击节奏，'Ordered Pairs II'的人声与中提琴对话接近自由即兴爵士的精神性，'Mirror Stage'则借循环与相位手法呼应简约主义对位技法。人声处理与器乐编织相互映照，结构简短却层次繁复，概念性与聆听美感并存。

items.body:
Psych duo Bear Bones, Lay Low naturally adapt to soundtrack dimensions with a richly atmospheric, electroacoustic accompaniment to Léonard Pongo’s titular film, benefitting from Laszlo Umbreit’s experience in this arena.

“Discrepant presents the LP edition of Tales from the Source, the original film soundtrack by Bear Bones, Lay Low and Laszlo Umbreit. Originally composed for Belgian-Congolese artist Léonard Pongo’s 2024 film of the same name, this release reworks the film's audio into a continuous, fluid listening experience.

The album is built on a direct contrast between heavy electronic manipulation and raw environmental audio. Laszlo Umbreit captured the foundation of the record through field recordings and additional electronics, focusing on the quiet, tactile sounds of water, riverbeds, and natural spaces. These recordings were then processed and expanded by Bear Bones, Lay Low, who layered the tracks using synthesizers, samplers and various effects processors.

Rather than acting as a standard background score, the music functions as a detailed piece of environmental sound art. The tracks are edited to blend into one another without distinct gaps, mirroring the slow pace and visual flow of the film. Through the use of tape loops, filtering, and electronic processing, the natural landscapes are systematically distorted and rearranged. The result is a dark, slow-moving suite of electroacoustic music that strips away traditional melody to focus entirely on texture, resonance, and the changing dynamics of the recorded environments.”
items._genre: electroacoustic / field recording / ambient / experimental / soundtrack
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是比利时-刚果艺术家Léonard Pongo同名电影的配乐，由双人组Bear Bones, Lay Low与Laszlo Umbreit合作完成。制作上首先由Umbreit通过田野录音捕捉河流、水体与自然空间的细微声响，再经Bear Bones, Lay Low使用合成器、采样器与多种效果器进行深度电子处理与重组。作品刻意消解传统旋律结构，将环境录音通过磁带循环、滤波与电子变形系统性地扭曲与重构，最终形成一套缓慢流动、质感密集的电声组曲。整张专辑被编辑为无明显停顿的连续聆听体验，呼应电影缓慢的视觉节奏，将环境声音艺术作为核心表达手段而非背景配乐。

items.album: Plenty Of Time With Nothing To Do

items.body:
Tobias Freund’s roots in ‘80s & ‘90s pop engineering - for Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf, Scatman John! - are touched-up in a 2nd parade of cover versions, of The Human League, This Heat, Japan, Suicide, Heaven 17, and Harold Budd & Brian Eno

Perhaps best known to many for his run of classic ’00s minimal techno as Tobias., the German producer’s binds run much deeper than that sound, with engineering credits on the likes of Lassigue Bendthaus’ pivotal EBM album ‘Matter’, as well as those that paid the bills (Milli Vanilli, Meat Loaf). ‘Plenty Of Time With Nothing To Do’ now catches him returning to formative passions with ample technical knowledge earned over the decades, generating a mix of faithful and daring takes on evergreens and personal faves augmented with inventive, playful nuance.

Tobias.’ freunds are vocal foils, with Barbie Williams perfectly emulating Andrea Conway’s dreamy delivery of Dome’s ‘Cruel When Complete’, subtly reset in dusty triplets, while Romina Schopf drily glazes the tribal groove of their take on This Heat’s ‘Twilight Furniture’, and Argenis Brito channels David Sylvian with a Latin accent in the re-do of Japan’s ‘My New Career’. The ‘floor is also attended on Gudrun Gut’s standout, breathy revision of Suicide’s ‘Girl’, and Tobias. himself even makes an appearance, pitched alien-like on a puckered revision of The Human League’s ‘Morale’, another highpoint along with Uwe Schmidt aka Atom™ reprising his LB ‘Pop Artificielle’ steez on a remake of Heaven 17’s ‘The Best Kept Secret’.
items._genre: electronic / post-punk / EBM / experimental pop / ambient
items._cn_summary: 德国制作人Tobias Freund在这张翻唱专辑中展现了他跨越数十年的音乐人脉与制作功底。专辑精选了The Human League、This Heat、Japan、Suicide、Heaven 17等后朋克与合成器流行经典，以techno的精密结构重新解构。Barbie Williams精确复刻了Dome的梦幻人声并融入碎拍律动，Romina Schopf在This Heat翻唱中铺设了部落化打击乐纹理，Argenis Brito以拉丁口音重新演绎David Sylvian的声线特质。Gudrun Gut对Suicide的翻唱以呼吸感人声重塑原曲，Atom™延续了Lassigue Bendthaus时期的电子美学。整体制作在忠于原作情绪的基础上，通过当代电子制作技术增添了实验性与解构色彩，是一次对八十至九十年代合成器美学的当代重译。

items.body:
Remastered reissue of This Heat’s hugely innovative and pioneering anti-rock classic, 1979,  this time on their own, eponymous label. A true milestone in the mutation of pop, rock, avant-garde and electronic music, and arguably post-punk's ground-zero, This Heat consolidated a wealth of music before its arrival whilst casting irrevocable influence over a generation of musicians, producers and engineers in its wake.

Formed in mid ‘70s Brixton, South London, around the trio of Charles Hayward, Charles Bullen and Gareth Williams (later of Flaming Tunes fame), the group drew on and experimented within a flux of sonic disciplines - concrète, pop, dub, and krautrock - to align their mutual ligaments and oppositional structures in a complex, dissonant mass of finely edited improvisations.

Spooling tape noise Testcards jar abruptly with bursts of taut, buzzing drums and metallic guitar squall in Horizontal Hold, before Williams appears as a lamenting ghost, wallowing in the funereal folk drone of Not Waving, and like Damo Suzuki’s shy opposite against the motorik flight of Twilight Furniture.

The album’s definitive moment is still to come, however, with the 2-bar lick of Hayward’s propulsive drums spun thru devilish reverbs and delays in the legendary 24 Track Loop marking a pivotal moment in flux between dub, punk and electro-acoustic music, before the record closes out with Fall of Saigon’s melancholy dirge pop, which clearly set a template for everyone from Hot Chip to Animal Collective or Micachu and the Shapes.

Perhaps understandably, This Heat were never intended as a commercial proposition but, thru the support of John Peel they were able to reach and beguile a national radio audience who probably weren’t ready for them. Thus, their boundary-oblivious virus was planted in the fertile minds of ’79, when punk had already eaten itself and new ideas were definitely required.

By using a minimalist, rhythmically-focussed palette, rent by great minds using the studio-as-instrument, This Heat represents a crucial transition or phase-shift in music from stratified styles toward a union of what might have been formerly perceived as mutually exclusive sounds or styles; boldly following a path out of genre restriction and dilating the dimensions of sonic possibility in the process.

A stone cold classic.
items._cn_summary: This Heat 1979年首张同名专辑由Charles Hayward、Charles Bullen与Gareth Williams在伦敦Brixton组建，将磁带噪音、具体音乐、dub与krautrock融为一炉，以极简节奏和精细剪辑的即兴手法，打破流派壁垒。唱片以磁带噪音与突发打击乐碰撞开场，随后沉入挽歌般的民谣嗡鸣；标志性的两小节鼓循环经由混响与延迟处理，跨越dub、朋克与电声音乐边界；终曲以忧郁行进曲式流行收束，被视为Hot Chip、Animal Collective等后辈的范本。评论指出该作将工作室作为乐器使用，代表了从分层风格向声音可能性扩张的关键转折，是后朋克与实验音乐的奠基之作。

items.album: Take me, I’m yours

items.body:
Jan Jelinek and Alan Abrahams of Portable/Bodycode fame come together on perhaps the most substantial new Jelinek project in years - recalling his own classic Gramm and Farben projects with this low-lit set of simmering, frayed House burners. Really stong!

The two were on each other's radars for years, but didn't come in contact properly until Abrahams brought Jelinek to play at one of his Süd Electronic parties, where they began to mull over the idea of a collaboration. Over the years, they built up a rapport; Abrahams would fire over material that Jelinek would work into the stems, slowly building up the confidence to take more and more risks. He began to fixate on Abrahams voice, ignoring the rest of the instrumentation and threaded it through his usual lattice of concrète sounds in a sort of classic Farben mode.

Farben's a good reference point, particularly for 'Forever', the set's housey-est cut. Jelinek explains in the accompanying press release that the raw vocal had reminded him of "classic house" and that's where we start, with jazzy keys gassing up Abrahams' soulful vox. By the time we hit the halfway point, Jelinek's processes have taken over, with buzzing synths and snowballing percussion that create a dense wall of insectoid noise and interference before the track fades dramatically to silence. It's the most propulsive material Jelinek's been involved with for ages; on '87BPM', he sways Abrahams' wordless groans into a trotting, ping pong shuffle and 'All One' does a thing with tape stop melodies and drunken vocals that sound like an offcut from the CMYK series of EPs.
items._cn_summary: Jan Jelinek 与 Alan Abrahams 合作呈现了一套低光环境下的电子作品，延续了 Jelinek 标志性的碎片化采样美学。会相聚于 Abrahams 主办的电子派对，两人逐步建立合作默契：Abrahams 先将素材发给 Jelinek，后者将人声从中剥离，编织入典型的拼贴式具象声音网格。制作手法上呼应其早期 Farben 时期的简约底色，混搭了灵魂人声、爵士键盘、嗡嗡作响的合成器声以及不断膨胀的打击乐层次，在中段逐渐堆叠成密集的蜂鸣噪声墙壁后戛然而止。'87BPM' 与 'All One' 分别展示了弹球节拍的律动摆动与磁带停止式的旋律处理，整体呈现出一种解构与重组并行的实验逻辑。

items.body:
As O.G. Jigg, Will “Memotone” Yates adapts his broad palette to the 16mm documentary and folk horror short imagery of Graham Vasey’s film project, The Black Tor, with an unmistakably vintage tone FFO Oskar Sala, Delia Derbyshire, Gruppo.

Named for the granite outcrop of Dartmoor, not too far from the musician’s native Bristol, ‘Black Tor Tracks’ depicts Yates in actual soundtrack mode, as opposed to imaginary. It gathers six instrumental accompaniments written between 2022-2026 that match the oneiric anachronisms of County Durham based Graham Vasey’s films with masterful blends of analog electronics and acoustic kit rendered in widescreen and dusted with a tone that reflects the filmmaker’s use of a 1950s Bolex and a 1930s Ensign Auto-Kinecam. 

If we weren’t informed otherwise, the music could easily pass for ‘50s or ’60 orchestral scores in a classic vein of British folk horror, or even Bernard Herrmann’s work for Hitchcock psychological thrillers - and by extension, even Oskar Sala in its electronic nuance - such is the timeless quality of Yates’ touch as O.G. Jigg. Severed from intended imagery the music remains potently synaesthetic, from the gloomy brood of ‘The Black Tor’, thru the celluloid dream sequence evocation of ‘The Sunken Kirk’, fine-wrought early electronic timbres of ‘Woodwose’ and ‘The Stones of Obb’, and hallucinatory tension of ‘Plough Stots’.

Good stuff.
items._genre: experimental electronic / soundtrack / analog synthesis / folk horror / vintage electronics
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Will Yates以O.G. Jigg为名，为Graham Vasey的16mm民俗恐怖短片项目《The Black Tor》创作的原声配乐，收录了2022至2026年间创作的六首器乐作品。Yates将模拟电子合成器与原声乐器进行融合，以宽屏化的音场营造出跨越时代的复古质感，听感上可与五十至六十年代英国民俗恐怖管弦乐配器、希区柯克心理惊悚片的Bernard Herrmann式弦乐、以及Oskar Sala的电子音色相提并论。专辑中的《The Black Tor》呈现阴沉的低压氛围，《The Sunken Kirk》唤起胶片梦境感，《Woodwose》与《The Stones of Obb》展现了精细的早期电子音色，《Plough Stots》则充满迷幻张力。即便脱离影像单独聆听，音乐本身仍具有强烈的通感效果，音画关系处理极为成熟，是当代独立实验配乐领域中兼具复古指向与声音实验性的作品。

items.body:
Dutch A/V duo Wanderwelle plunge Davey Jones’ locker in a richly metaphoric expression of worries about climate change and marine devastation, blending hydrophonic acoustic and electronic sources to spell out a sonorous, subaquatic narrative FFO Mark Jenkin film scores, Thomas Köner, AFX’s SAW II...

“After All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea (2023) and Black Clouds Above The Bows (2022), Amsterdam-based collective Wanderwelle presents the final entry of their album trilogy for Important Records (IMPREC). Conceived as a sonic reflection on the climate crisis and its devastating impact on coastal ecosystems, Ghosts Beneath The Brine (2026) addresses the mass deaths of fish, seabirds, crustaceans and countless other creatures that call these seas home, now rapidly being overfished, warming and acidifying.

Where antique cavalry trumpets played a central role on Black Clouds Above The Bows and a dying church organ shaped All Hands Bury The Cliffs At Sea, cymbals form the core of Ghosts Beneath The Brine. The instruments were submerged in seawater for extended periods of time and played with a bow at various stages of corrosion. As the bronze alloy gradually reacted with the saltwater, their sound transformed, becoming darker, more fragile and unstable. Over time, the metal began to sing in ghostly overtones, as if haunted by the waters that shaped it. Much like large groups of fish shimmering beneath the surface, the cymbals slowly lost their shine, both sonically and physically, as salt and time took hold.

Alongside its environmental narrative, the album draws from maritime mythology. Echoes of the sea bishop, the kraken, devil whales and sea serpents emerge throughout its soundscape. Once feared and revered, these creatures now exist only in the liminal space between folklore and memory, haunting the collective imagination like omens from a forgotten age. Through immersive textures and submerged harmonies, Wanderwelle intertwines myth and mourning, inviting listeners to drift between the real and the spectral. If humanity continues on its current course, familiar species such as sharks, oysters and even gulls may soon share the same fate as their legendary predecessors, becoming ghosts beneath the brine.”
items._genre: experimental / ambient / dark ambient / electroacoustic / sound art
items._cn_summary: Wanderwelle 是来自阿姆斯特丹的视听组合，2026年发行的《Ghosts Beneath The Brine》是其专辑三部曲的终章，延续了前作对气候危机的关注。整张专辑围绕海洋生态崩溃展开叙事，鱼群、海鸟、甲壳类因过度捕捞、海水升温与酸化大量死亡。为获取核心声响，组合将铙钹长时间浸入海水，以弓拉奏不同腐蚀阶段的金属——合金与盐水反应后音色逐渐变暗、变脆，泛音如同被海水附灵的幽响。专辑同时融入海主教、北海巨妖、魔鬼鲸等海洋神话形象，在神话与哀悼之间编织沉浸式质感。整体手法将声学物件、hydrophonic录音与电子处理结合，呈现出兼具环境音景与暗潮氛围的实验声响作品。

items.album: Forced to Feel
items.artist: Eyal Maoz, Piero Bittolo Bon, Zeno De Rossi
items.excerpt: Improvised free music recording develops around some recurring patterns: the single event in which musicians group, play and then disperse – the recording freezes a moment in time; the long term association – each recording a moment in a sequence sometimes with the risk of developing idioms, of creating a comfort zone at the expense of creative freedom; or a core of frequent collaborators meet a guest / guests - in this case the embryo of an idiom is here but it is tested and mutated by the newc
items.body: Improvised free music recording develops around some recurring patterns: the single event in which musicians group, play and then disperse – the recording freezes a moment in time; the long term association – each recording a moment in a sequence sometimes with the risk of developing idioms, of creating a comfort zone at the expense of creative freedom; or a core of frequent collaborators meet a guest / guests - in this case the embryo of an idiom is here but it is tested and mutated by the newcomers. Forced to Feel offers still another possibility being recorded after the group has “already tested its chemistry on stage (…) at a moment of deepened trust and heightened risk, refining a shared language forged in performance and now pushed further in the studio” (linear notes). What I understand is that they are on their way to create an idiom but are still willing to experiment and take risks… their language is still a virus. Eyal Maoz (electric guitar), Piero Bittolo Bon (alto and baritone sax, shakuhachi, electronics), and Zeno De Rossi (drums, bells) all come to this meeting from different directions with Bittolo Bon and De Rossi having played together many times in many different contexts, and the results are intense. A meaningful use of electronics, a sort of underground groove that flows into this sonic universe, splinters of melody scattered into the noise. In the opening piece, Renato’s 'Arcade,' a set of electronic sounds coming directly from a 1980s arcade creates a foundation on which De Rossi builds his texture and Maoz and Bittolo Bon display their fragments of melodies. Music then evolves into a more pensive mood in 'Invoking the Ancestors' - the guitar provides a net of arpeggios and fragmented melodies while percussions, bells and electronics create a field for the alto sax to play a eerie song that dissolves into itself. In 'Nervous Butterflies' a quasi unison of electronics, sax and guitar open the piece developing a swarm of circular motives that evolve one into the other with the addition of the percussion. Something like a jazz-rock guitar emerges over a riff just to develop into angular sounds that seem nostalgic of other times. The drum than brings the sax into a jazzy atmosphere that seems to freeze into the end. 'Moon Hovering' builds on an obsessive percussive patterns and offers the possibility to mark the essential contribution that De Rossi offers to the trio creating a unifying but open and volatile design that enriches sense of global improvisation. The same may be true for 'Part Hypnosis' where the three musicians seem to find a place of their own. The baritone sax develops an obsessive melody in 'Flickering Wings,' this slowly changes into a deconstructed blues, sometimes some electronic noise adds an ironic note to prepare the finale with De Rossi again in evidence. 'Pull Me into the Blue Water' contains all of the elements presented so far with the addition of the shakuhachi flute that adds rarefaction to the mix. The guitar reacts with dreamy sonorities, the drum marks its path with a sense of necessity. That’s it. After many listening sessions, I feel that all of the fragments, the different sounds, the different attitudes gather into sonic nebulas each with its distinctive features but with an overall inner coherence. Undetermined and yet beautiful. You can listen to and download the digital album on bandcamp. forced to feel by Eyal Maoz, Piero Bittolo Bon & Zeno de Rossi Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free improvisation / experimental jazz / electronic / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由电吉他手Eyal Maoz、萨克斯/尺八/电子乐手Piero Bittolo Bon以及鼓手Zeno De Rossi组成的三重奏录制，创作根基在于现场演出中积累的默契与信任。评论指出，乐队尚未形成固定语汇，仍处于实验与冒险阶段，乐句如病毒般不断变异。电子元素被巧妙地编织进声音宇宙，形成一种地下律动，旋律碎片散落于噪音之中。开场曲以1980年代街机电子音效为底，鼓手在此铺设织体，吉他与萨克斯呈现旋律碎片。第二曲转向沉思氛围，吉他琶音与打击乐、电子音效构成场域，让中音萨克斯奏出诡异旋律并自我消解。后半部分乐队尝试准齐奏、爵士摇滚段落与蓝调解构等手法，尺八的加入则为终曲增添稀薄感。整体来看，这是一次在即兴框架内融合电子、噪音与自由爵士元素的探索，文本对每首曲目的结构与变化进行了详细描述。

items.body: Label: Self released, 2026 Personnel - Gon Muruaga: electric guitar; Camila Nebbia: tenor saxophone; Jonathan Bäckström: double bass; Teemu Mustonen: drums. Gon Muruaga is an Argentinian guitarist and composer based in Helsinki, Finland. Unafraid of taking risks, Muruaga plays with open forms and fragmentation in a mix of aural explosions and quietly composed atmospheres, joining forces with fellow countrywoman Camila Nebbia on saxophone (a prominent figure in the free-improvisation scene) and the Finnish rhythm section of bassist Jonathan Bäckström and drummer Teemu Mustonen. Freefalling Latitude opens with “ Latifall ”, where Nebbia’s tenor descriptions trace geometric figures and sharp angles. Loose drums and bold guitar accompaniment support her unconditionally, while the bass enters late yet confidently. Muruaga pushes the electronic side of his instrument to the fore, employing delay effects while exploring skronky, clustered sounds. “ Fogradient ” has ethereal guitar waves contributing to the initial ambient texture, yet we can hear Bäckström’s bass lines pulsating in the background. There’s uncertainty within a spatial mist and formless void, but things gradually build toward a roaring climax. This alternation between rumination and eruption is a constant throughout. If “ Gyroslip ” features jarring, rusty guitar attacks, swift saxophone runs, and a lumpy, tribal-like groove underneath, “ Paralaxial ” and “ Isoplex ” investigate balmy sonic possibilities, whether through finespun percussion and unyielding yet mysterious harmonic contours or saxophone overtones and non-abrasive atmospheric friction. These are musicians who listen closely to one another, and “ Nebulode ” brings them together to unearth new sounds as part of the quartet’s exploratory aesthetic. Out of a maze of fragmentation, the band finds a raw connection through clattering percussion and inharmonic collisions. Its wry experimental vision remains engaging, keeping our ears wide open. Curiously, there’s something invigorating about this quartet, but also the lingering feeling that it is capable of achieving even more. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Latifall ► 04 - Gyroslip ► 05 - Nebulode
items._genre: free improvisation / experimental jazz / avant-garde / electronic
items._cn_summary: 这是由阿根廷吉他手Gon Muruaga领衔、现居赫尔辛基创作的四重奏专辑，四位成员分别来自阿根廷与芬兰，形成跨国编制。整张作品以开放结构和碎片化为核心手法，在听觉爆发与静谧氛围之间不断切换。电吉他使用延迟效果探索粗粝的集群音色和电子化处理，萨克斯则以几何线条般的旋律在空间中勾勒轮廓，低音大鼓迟缓进入却充满信心，鼓手则以节奏碎片为整体注入不确定感。贝斯线条在背景中脉动，吉他声波营造出迷雾般的氛围质地，逐步推向高潮。专辑中既有尖锐碰撞的不和谐声响，也有圆润的泛音与不具侵略性的摩擦感，体现出演奏者之间密切的倾听关系。最终在混乱的碎片中寻得原始连接，以敲击式打击乐和非谐波碰撞作为出口，展现出一种冷幽默的实验美学。

items.body: Grief is a universal experience that no one can truly be prepared for, and one that each of us inhabits differently, in ways we are unable to control or predict. Written for Paula Ďurinová’s film Lapilli, Petra Hermanova‘s soundtrack follows an exploration of death through stones, caves and volcanic landscapes, asking how the physical world absorbs and preserves traces of loss. The title refers to the fragments of rock ejected during a volcanic eruption—small stones suspended between destruction and renewal—and Hermanová’s music inhabits that same uncertain territory, poised between fragility and endurance. The opening suite, “Five Stages”, moves at a measured pace, every gesture carrying its full weight without ever tipping into emotional excess. Rather than illustrating the five stages of grief to which the title presumably alludes, the music creates a contemplative space in which listeners are left to negotiate that process for themselves, offering emotional cues without ever prescribing a response. Pieces such as “Outcome (Massives)” and “Soft Void” shift the focus towards resonance, silence and the physical behaviour of sound itself. Broken autoharps, their cracked strings given one final voice, merge with the film’s environmental soundscape until it becomes difficult to distinguish music from water droplets, stone or air. Each sound seems pared back to its essence, as though carved from rock rather than composed. By degrees the textures thicken and subtle trajectories begin to emerge, most clearly in “The Cave”, before “Dusk, Breath” brings the work to a close, the organ lending the final moments a quiet, almost liturgical sense of resolution. If In Death’s Eyes confronted bereavement as an intimate human wound, Lapilli broadens that perspective, suggesting that grief belongs as much to landscapes and geological time as it does to ourselves. Rather than offering consolation, Hermanová creates a place where mourning is simply allowed to continue, carried by stone, air and the slow passage of time. In the following interview conducted via email Petra Hermanova elaborates on her production process. Both In Death’s Eyes, your previous album and Lapilli are deeply concerned with death, grief, and transformation, but they seem to approach those themes from different angles. In In Death’s Eyes, death often appears as an intimate, almost bodily presence, whereas Lapilli explores loss through rocks, caves, minerals, and geological time. Did working on Paula Ďurinová’s film change the way you think about death? Did it shift your focus from personal grief toward a broader relationship between mortality, landscape, and material transformation? The way I think about death was most significantly changed by experiencing the death of a loved one. Anything that came afterwards was more damage control. Paula and I went through a grieving process around the same time, and we also worked on our debuts in parallel. When I was in the Merseburg Cathedral recording organ for my album, Paula was descending deep inside of cave systems to film for her documentary, and we kept texting each other photographs of these incredible spaces. They were profound experiences and I remember quite clearly that life made sense again in those moments, the pain was transmuted. I tried to think about working on my album as a way of contributing to the canon of music dealing with human mortality, but it still ended up being a very personal work. I came to a different understanding with Lapilli. Having been invited to write music for someone else’s reckoning with death, I got to observe a separate grieving process. Suddenly there were different associations, metaphors and coping mechanisms in place, and this was a much stronger departure from the personal to the universal. The autoharp plays a central role in both works, yet its function feels different. On In Death’s Eyes, it often acts as the voice of the individual sufferer, standing in tension with the transcendence of the pipe organ. On Lapilli, the autoharp seems to become part of the landscape itself, with its detuned and deteriorating strings echoing caves, stone, and erosion. How did your relationship with the instrument evolve between these two projects, and what drew you to its increasingly fragile and material qualities? Autoharp is a matter close to my heart, maybe more of an obsession. I always feel a bit sad that I can only ever bring two with me while I’m performing because they are all so different. Writing music for film is more free in this aspect, and so my first thought was to use the broken autoharps in my collection, the ones that I don’t dare to restring and tune properly, because they’re too fragile, too cracked. There is an analogy somewhere in there about the possibilities of someone who feels fragile and broken but still would like to be useful. I thought a lot about instruments that are no longer played and just lay somewhere, completely mute. Even one of my main instruments hung on a wall somewhere in Spandau for decades, before I got it. So it was about seeing what kind of sounds can be still coaxed out of these “dead” autoharps, and this couldn’t be further away from how I usually write music. There is a peculiar sports event called the Autoharp Toss in which participants of a musical gathering compete in tossing an autoharp beyond repair as far as they can. Instead of that, I took these autoharps and recorded their swan songs. Lapilli is the soundtrack to “a soft film about hard matter” and the liner notes ask how rocks, pebbles, and mountains die. The music often feels suspended between human memory and geological time, as if grief is being measured against processes far older than ourselves. When composing the music, were you trying to sonify the landscape itself, or were the sounds primarily a way of reflecting the emotional journey of the film’s narrator through loss? Lapilli is now a music release, but in the film it exists alongside the sound design Paula worked on with the composer and musician Agnese Menguzzato. In places they are so intertwined, that it can be difficult to distinguish what is music and what is sound design—in the caves, the pluck of an autoharp string may as well be the sound of a water drop. We talked at great lengths about all these scenes and what they represent. I am a very visual person, so while it sometimes felt a little bit like looking for the sound of the landscape, or of all these various geological processes the landscapes undergo, most often we were working in more abstract terms, superimposing sonic parallels onto fragments of text or mental states that informed these scenes. As the film moves through its stages, the instrumentation develops a narrative also, and the broken autoharps are at first accompanied, and then slowly replaced with the steady breath of an organ. In In Death’s Eyes, lyrics played a crucial role in articulating grief, uncertainty, and the tension between spiritual and earthly forms of consolation. Lapilli, by contrast, communicates almost entirely through instrumental sound, texture, and space. Did working on a film allow you to express things that language couldn’t? How different was it to construct meaning through timbre, resonance, and silence rather than through words and song? By the time I started composing for Lapilli, I had been working with the theme of death for almost two years. I saw it as an opportunity to extend and inhabit the same space with similar means, but with a very different set of constraints and reasons for them. In my practice, the usual starting point is silence. I then fill the silence with as little as I can, or as much as I want to. This time, the starting point was an already emotionally saturated image with an equally charged narration, so I had to construct different poetic principles for this work. How much can I add without overloading this moment? How sparse can I go—and will it still be music then? Previously I hadn’t considered making purely instrumental music, so this was pivotal, it opened a new channel for me. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: Petra Hermanová 为 Paula Ďurinová 的影片《Lapilli》创作配乐，标题源自火山喷发抛出的岩石碎片，暗示毁灭与新生之间的悬置状态。音乐以缓慢的节奏展开，通过破碎的自动竖琴、风琴和环境音景相互渗透，将水滴、石头与空气的声响融入作品，使音乐与环境录音的边界变得模糊。作品围绕死亡、哀悼与地质时间展开，呈现出沉思式的聆听空间，不强加情感反应，而是让哀伤在石头、空气与缓慢的时间流逝中持续存在。从个人化的亲密悲痛转向更广阔的自然与物质视角，展现了声音作为物质本身的雕塑性特质。

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — The birth of this new album was marked by difficult personal events and major changes within the band. In 2019, longtime co-founder Scott Kelly permanently left the group after serious domestic issues. This led Neurosis into a long period of pause and reflection. For this new phase, core members Steve Von Till, Jason Roeder, Dave Edwardson and Noah Landis enthusiastically welcomed Aaron Turner, a leading figure in post-metal, already frontman of Isis and Sumac, as the new guitarist and vocalist. Turner fit in perfectly, actively contributing to the songwriting with his creativity and talent. The album was recorded by producer Scott Evans in a fast process that resulted in an extremely raw sound.The album, speaks of spiritual and emotional survival in a difficult time, both globally and personally. The title itself sets, on one side, the image of a world on fire, a symbol of the environmental and geopolitical crises around us; on the other, the strength of love, which endures despite everything. This "burning world" also represents the hardships the band faced after Scott Kelly's departure, a time of great change and pain. The "undying love," instead, is the choice not to give up, to keep believing in empathy, love and the beauty of art, even when everything seems to fall apart. The album doesn't stick to pure violence, but also plays with tension and silence. Noah Landis has a key role, adding spectral synthesizers, industrial noises and samples that recall the darker Pink Floyd. Many tracks unfold through long, ritual crescendos, like the closing suite "Last Light" (17 minutes), which gradually turns into an industrial escalation.Aaron Turner, with his deep, cavernous and abstract growl, pairs perfectly with Steve Von Till's desperate screams. Alternating with these two voices are bassist Dave Edwardson's deep choruses and ghostly spoken word, creating a true tragic chorus that perfectly tells the story of the world's collapse."An Undying Love for a Burning World" is an album that grabs you right away, with its emotional charge and bold sonic choices. There are moments that struck me in particular.The album's opening is truly unforgettable for the intense emotional weight it conveys, a goosebump-inducing start. The instrumental introduction "We Are Torn Wide Open" builds an almost cinematic tension. The industrial drones and tribal tolls give a sense of emptiness and looming danger.In "Mirror Deep," halfway through the track, the music slows down, almost stops, creating a suspended atmosphere, then explodes into a section of incredible heaviness. It's right at this moment that Aaron Turner screams the line "True wealth between our fingers slip, as we count the dead". A passage that fuses the melancholic force of post-metal with a shattering impact. Noah Landis's synths take the track to near-spatial levels.Then there's "Blind": the central instrumental section opens into stretched, hypnotic dynamics, recalling the more psychedelic Pink Floyd and krautrock, slowing the pace and leaving room for the music. The following contrast, between clean vocals and powerful growls over an imposing wall of guitars, is one of the album's most intense and surprising passages."Seething and Scattered" has direct, syncopated riffs full of tension, spilling into an unexpected rhythmic turn. Jason Roeder's drumming creates an almost tribal atmosphere before the track heads into spectacular progressions.Finally, the ending of "Last Light" (a 17-minute suite), a colossal suite that closes with the desperate, anguished cry "What have we done?", which fades into a loop of industrial noise, drones and feedback.This album is undoubtedly a masterpiece. Turner didn't just replace Scott Kelly; he became a true creative engine, bringing his deep growl and his unique approach. It's not a nostalgia move, but a work that shows how Neurosis are still the kings of post-metal, able to reinvent themselves and rise even from major personal hardships.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑诞生于乐队核心成员Scott Kelly离队后的艰难时期，Aaron Turner（Isis/Sumac主创）的加入为乐队注入新血。制作人Scott Evans以快速录制保留了极端粗糙的原始质感。专辑主题围绕燃烧世界中对不灭之爱的信念，融合了精神层面的生存叙事。音乐上不仅依赖重型音墙，还大量运用张力与静默的对比：Noah Landis贡献了幽冥合成器、工业噪音与采样，呈现出黑暗Pink Floyd式的氛围。曲目以仪式感的长篇渐强为结构，17分钟的终曲展现工业化的逐层升级。Turner深沉的咆哮与Von Till绝望的嘶喊交替出现，配合Edwardson的低沉合唱与幽灵般的念白，形成悲剧性的声部交织。多首作品在悬停与爆发之间剧烈切换，情感冲击力强烈。

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — "Let's THRAK Again" is a tribute to the 1995 album THRAK by King Crimson, with the approval and blessing of founder Robert Fripp. This album is Stick Men's first studio record in over ten years, a project that brings together two longtime members of King Crimson's rhythm section from that era, bassist Tony Levin and drummer Pat Mastelotto, along with Touch Guitar virtuoso Markus Reuter.The trio wanted to recreate the same controlled chaos and the energy of the original album, describing it as "instrumental chamber music". They composed and arranged the twelve tracks to be performed live as a lean trio, with minimal use of sampling or electronics.To offer a truly unique experience, the band decided not to release just one mix, but two completely different versions of the same recorded material. The first, Reel One, mixed by Stefano Castagna, follows a track sequence devised by Tony Levin, focusing on a very specific sonic vision and philosophy. The second, Reel Two (yet to be released), mixed by Fabio Trentini, will feature a different sequence, curated by Mastelotto and Reuter, and uses (they say) entirely new sound choices and audio approaches. All tracks are previously unreleased compositions, recorded specifically for this project. The trio described the whole work as a series of pieces created from scratch to develop an "original sonic vocabulary".Stick Men themselves described the album's musical style as "heavy prog with nothing short of explosive kinetic energy", and I agree with that definition. A sound that blends the typical elements of darker, more mathematical progressive rock with industrial, art rock and avant-garde metal influences. The songs have intricate structures and odd time signatures, driven by powerful, massive riffs. Even though they're only three, the simultaneous combination of melodic lines and a rocky bass creates a dense, intense orchestral sound.The album alternates moments of pure instrumental acceleration with softer, more rarefied ambient passages, keeping a tense and always experimental atmosphere. The rhythm section blends the power of acoustic sounds with industrial samples, loops and electronic pads.My favorite tracks are: "Swimming in Tea", which is without a doubt the track that surprised me the most, chosen as the lead single, with an immediate structure and the special feature of having Markus Reuter on vocals, before giving way to a memorable Tony Levin Chapman Stick solo.The opening track, "Let's THRAK Again", for its ability to reproduce the complex rhythms and the "heavy prog" impact that distinguished the original 1995 King Crimson album."Haggin Triptych", an instrumental suite divided into three parts (Renoir, Carriage Parade and Yosemite Sunset), which is a masterful example of rhythmic interlocking. A triumphant and thrilling return, a true masterpiece of composition and musical performance, a must-buy for both King Crimson devotees and lovers of heavier avant-prog. Essential album.
items._genre: heavy prog / avant-prog / progressive rock / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑向King Crimson 1995年专辑THRAK致敬，由贝斯手Tony Levin、鼓手Pat Mastelotto与触摸吉他演奏家Markus Reuter三人组合创作。整张专辑以三重奏形式重新构建原专辑的"受控混乱"理念，十二首原创作品均专为该项目录制。专辑以Reel One形式先期发行，由Stefano Castagna混音，采用Tony Levin设计的曲目序列，强调声学乐器与工业采样、循环、电子音色的融合。音乐风格融合暗色调数学前卫摇滚、工业、art rock与前卫金属元素，结构复杂且充满不规则拍子，在器乐加速段落与稀疏氛围段落之间交替，制造持续紧张的实验氛围。专辑中"Swimming in Tea"出人意料地加入了人声，随后展开Levin的Chapman Stick独奏；"Haggin Triptych"则是一首分为三个乐章的器乐组曲，展示三人节奏的精密咬合。

items.body: This is an ultimate record for the record collecting heads. Denver’s Osmium House project always mixes together elements of the most far reaching and eclectic corners of the psychedelic music universe. Elements of kosmische musik, library records and esoteric 70s film scores and more can be felt throughout Aesop Adams’ work like strange Ley lines surging through release to release. On his latest album, Dawn Club, he handcrafted mesmerizing synth and guitar-based soundscapes at home directly to tape, and the end results sound like a cult private press cassette that is half-way between early New Age music and early Bobby Beausoleil outtakes. On this tape, now available through Island House Recordings, Adams operates totally solo while utilizing everything from guitars, bass and lap harp to synthesizers, tubular bells, drum machines and more. A total jack-of-all trades, Adams expertly harnessed this cache of instruments to generate the most eerie, atmospheric and dreamlike bed of dronescapes he could. With audible tape hiss, warble and other lo-fi elements to the production (with some outside mixing help by Andrew Weathers, who also mastered the album), the record feels like it was ripped directly from a VHS copy of a lost DIY horror film in the most pleasing of ways. Murky, transportive and always rich with texture, mood and a thick mushroomy haze, Dawn Club is perhaps Adams at his most ambient, with rippling pools of vintage Casios and shimmering wind chimes. Kosmische musik doesn’t always have to be loud or grandiose. Sometimes, like on this tape, it can be subtle, restrained and leaning heavily upon tone to conjure alien worlds and expanded frames of mind. Listen to this tape closely with an open imagination, and you’ll surely find yourself traveling to places previously untrodden. Grab your copy from Island House today. -KH
items._genre: ambient / kosmische musik / lo-fi drone / experimental electronic
items._cn_summary: Denver音乐人Aesop Adams的Osmium House项目以一人之力完成了这张磁带专辑的创作，跨越迷幻宇宙音乐、图书馆录音与七十年代邪典电影配乐等多重领域。他在家庭环境中使用吉他、贝斯、膝琴、合成器、管钟、鼓机等多样乐器，直接录制到磁带，构建出迷离而充满氛围感的声场。Andrew Weathers负责混音与母带处理，使得成品保留了明显的磁带嘶声、抖动及其他低保真元素，营造出从VHS录像带中提取出的独立恐怖电影配乐般的质感。琴音、暗色氛围与怀旧合成器音色交织，专辑呈现克制的氛围倾向，不依赖音量与宏大叙事，而是通过音色与质感召唤异世界图景。整张作品带有浓厚的私密出版气质，适合在开放式聆听中探索未知的声音地带。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Some release an album a month, while others release an EP every couple of years. art test belongs to the latter group. 2024’s fever dreams collected a series of carefully curated singles, and 2026’s foreign lands does the same, acting as a tiny mix tape. The instrumental hip-hop timbre remains in full effect, while the focus is on Middle Eastern rhythms, a purposeful nod to current events. “across the oil fields” is especially timely in its title and bittersweet tone. The world continues to rely on oil, the control continues to shift hands, and art test conveys the melancholic undercurrent of a person who has seen the same scenarios play out again and again, generation after generation. The title track offers its own semantic twist; to Western nations, the Middle East is comprised of “foreign lands,” while the opposite is true when the perspectives are flipped. The track combines Western beats with Eastern strings, offering a third alternative. Older readers may remember a similar time in music, around the turn of the century, when empathy for people around the world was translated into dance music. In the modern era, the very idea of a “ceasefire” seems open to interpretation. Over the past few weeks, many have been called, many have been broken, and some have been broken while the antagonists have insisted that they have not. The entire system of negotiation is flawed. In the track of the same name, optimism is replaced by forlorn resignation, emphasizing the “down” in “downtempo.” By ending in “plumes of smoke,” art test communicates trepidation, but the very existence of the music is a testimony of hope. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: instrumental hip-hop / world fusion / downtempo / electronic
items._cn_summary: art test 延续了精选单曲合辑的发行模式，将器乐嘻哈音色与中东节奏作为核心切入点。专辑以'foreign lands'为题，探讨东西方视角的翻转与错位——在西方眼中中东是'异域'，反之亦然，这种语义双关贯穿全作。音乐层面将西方节拍与东方弦乐并置，试图在两种文化逻辑之间构建第三种可能。'across the oil fields'以苦乐参半的基调映射石油地缘政治的循环；同名曲中乐观被无奈取代，强化了 downtempo 中'低沉'一词的情感重量。结尾的'plumes of smoke'传递出不安与忧虑，但音乐本身的存在仍构成对希望的见证。整张专辑延续了千禧年前后那种将共情注入舞曲的传统，在当下语境中显得格外应景。

items.body: Review by James007 — The Watcher I've had a week to listen to this album on EKGPulse and I have to admit I was wrong. When the album was announced, I thought "great, another listenable effort from Eric." I had purchased and enjoyed his previous albums. His work on excellent prog gems like "Lost", "Godspeed", and "Escape" all provided a backdrop of solid craftmanship and technical brilliance with the anticipation of the next chapter along those lines. I was wrong. This was the next level. Perhaps hanging around with Neal and Randy and Mike and Diego helped.... maybe. I'll admit to being an EK "homer" because of his participation in NMB and Temic, but I did not expect THIS. There is true genius in this record. The Overture paints such a wonderful tone to start the album and as each movement takes flight to leave its mark you know you'll be listening to this album again and again. When "The One That Sees It All Alive" hits, the brilliance of this record is finally revealed. The coda of "Fade to Stillness" completes the journey with a sense of peace. The melodies throughout this record are next level greatness. The fact that EK plays everything on this album reminds me of the first time I listened to Jon Anderson's "Olias of Sunhillow" and the awe revealed in one person's inspiration and genius. Yeah, I was wrong. I listen to a bunch of Prog.... in fact, that's about all I listen to. This is a top 3 Prog album for 2026. I'd stack this one up against anything I've heard this year... anything. Yeah, I was wrong. And I pray I'm wrong again and again. Nicely done, sir.
items._genre: progressive metal / instrumental prog / technical metal
items._cn_summary: Eric Gillette 独立完成整张专辑的所有乐器演奏，呈现出概念专辑式的连贯结构。专辑以《The Overture》开场奠定氛围基调，随后各乐章依次展开旋律叙事，《The One That Sees It All Alive》被视为整张作品的高光段落，而终曲《Fade to Stillness》的尾声段以平静收束完成整体旅程。评论者将其与 Jon Anderson 独立完成的《Olias of Sunhillow》类比，强调一人创作所呈现的灵感密度与编曲完整性。音乐延续了 Gillette 此前作品的技艺底色，但在旋律构思与段落编排层面被评价为更进一步的突破。

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — The Aether are an instrumental project from Milan that is making waves with its third studio album, a record that marks a real turning point in their journey begun in 2021. This new work explores a fascinating sonic territory, a refined blend of progressive rock, Northern European jazz-rock, Canterbury sounds, post-rock and ambient electronica.In 2026, with Luminol Records, "III" arrived, the album of maturity, closing a trilogy of instrumental avant-garde. After the post-rock debut of 2023 and the cosmic atmospheres of "Trans-Neptunian Objects" (2024), the quartet ? made up of Andrea Ferrari, Andrea Grumelli, Andrea Serino and Teo Ravelli ? decided to explore a more human and instinctive dimension, setting aside complex concepts.In 2025, the band isolated themselves for long sessions of collective improvisation, minimizing pre-packaged writing. To capture the spontaneous energy typical of jazz bands, they chose to record everything live, with no digital editing or computer fixes. The raw tracks were then refined, mixed and mastered while keeping intact the original punchy dynamics, a blend of the Canterbury sound and Northern European jazz.During the post-production of "Vogon", the band decided to add a touch of originality by involving Claudio Milano, for an avant-garde vocal performance in recitar cantando. Added to this are the flute contributions by Rosarita Crisafi in the opening track "Oort Cloud". These collaborations define the album's experimental and choral nature."III" is an album that plays with expectations, abandoning the classic narrative structure of a concept album to dive into abstraction, into "continuous flow" and into the very essence of the human being, and it invites an inner journey, discovering spontaneity and the "self-generative power" of music.A river of sounds flowing nonstop, with no precise destination. That's exactly the effect created by the music of "III": abstract, fluid, a collective stream born from the 2025 improvisations. The tracks evoke mental landscapes, ranging from cinematic atmospheres to meditative silences and sudden bursts of chaotic, distorted energy. A bit like a film unfolding in our mind, with images following one another in an unpredictable harmony.The album gives great importance to silence and to the resonances between notes, using silence as a blank space on which music can paint, creating a unique and evocative atmosphere.But the real concept of "III" is human interaction, the magic that happens when musicians play together in the same room. No algorithms, no hyper-edited computer music: here live expressiveness is valued, the spontaneous mistake, the musicians' physical togetherness. An authentic, engaging experience that conveys all the energy of the moment.Even though instrumental, the album evokes conceptual suggestions through the titles and the few textual inserts. Take for example "Panta Rei", which translates into music Heraclitus' philosophical idea that "everything flows", constantly changing shape, starting from a jazz opening and flowing into a hypnotic ending. Or "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince", a tribute to Saint-Exup�ry's work, trying to capture the poetic loneliness and innocence of the Little Prince. And then there's "Vogon", a track inspired by the alien race from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, with Claudio Milano's avant-garde voice reciting a cryptic text, the only explicit literary element in a sea of instrumental sounds."III" is a record that tastefully blends modern progressive rock, European jazz and instrumental post-rock. It's almost entirely instrumental, acoustic and analog, and it stands out for a crazy dynamism, with moments of deep silence alternating with scream-worthy sonic explosions.The influence of Northern European jazz is felt right away in the handling of space and silence. The open chords of the Fender Rhodes and the laid-back bass lines create ethereal, suspended atmospheres.The band takes up the rhythmic complexity and odd meters typical of classic progressive rock (Soft Machine and King Crimson), but without sounding nostalgic or like a copy.Many tracks develop with long crescendos typical of modern post-rock, where layers of distorted guitars and minimal electronics build up until they culminate in imposing, hypnotic finales that leave you speechless.The analog warmth of the Fender Rhodes electric piano and the fretless bass creates a soft, jazzy harmonic bed that wraps around you.The Chapman Stick makes it possible to combine complex bass lines and geometric textures, adding a unique touch to the sound.The guitar ranges from clean, cinematic arpeggios to powerful distortions that give you goosebumps. The drums don't just keep time, but constantly interact with the other instruments, integrating subtle electronic nuances that enrich the whole.The album mainly moves between Jazz-Rock and contemporary Progressive Rock. Being an experimental work in constant evolution, it sits at the crossroads of three major musical genres:Avant-Prog / Progressive Rock, for the complexity of its structures, the use of odd meters and the long instrumental suites that recall the historic Canterbury Scene.Modern Jazz (ECM School), for the strong improvisational component, the use of open, warm chords and a handling of silence typical of Northern European jazz.Instrumental and Cinematic Post-Rock, for the development of the tracks through atmospheric dynamics and long "crescendos" that culminate in imposing walls of distorted guitars and minimal electronics.A modern formula that combines the refined technique of jazz with the visceral power of alternative rock.In my opinion, three tracks from "III" stand out as the most representative of the album:Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres, with the excellent interplay between electric guitar and Fender Rhodes, managing to create exotic, hypnotic atmospheres without overdoing the virtuosity.La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince, the calmest and most ambient track, with the skillful use of atmospheric electronics and a cultured, pianistic approach.Vogon, the most disorienting and original piece. Even if it breaks with the record's completely instrumental nature thanks to Claudio Milano's avant-garde recitar cantando, it shows experimental courage and a strong theatrical charge."III" is an album that invites active listening, letting yourself be carried by the flow of the music and discovering the endless possibilities hidden between the notes. A unique, unforgettable experience that will leave you wanting to listen again and again. Excellent album!

items._cn_summary: 来自米兰的器乐乐队 The Aether 推出第三张录音室专辑，作为三部曲的终章，乐队放弃了概念专辑的叙事结构，转向集体即兴与现场同期录音的方式，刻意保留演奏中的自发错误与原始力度。整张作品追求声音的连续流动，不预设目的地——既有电影化的氛围铺设，也有突如其来的失真爆发，静默被作为留白处理，与音符共振形成独特张力。在后摇滚、北欧爵士摇滚与坎特伯雷声响的基础上，专辑邀请人声实验与长笛参与，增添了前卫合唱的质感。专辑强调人类互动的核心价值：同处一室的演奏、未经算法修饰的鲜活表达，以及音乐自发的生成力量，将赫拉克利特的哲学思想转化为听觉景观。

items.body: When we first heard Analog Dance’s recent single Fall Apart, the song seemed built from passion and pressure: a rigid beat marking the perimeter, bright synthesizers narrowing the available space, and Jonny Castle’s baritone holding its composure while the dancefloor threatens to bend and buckle from its seductive groove. Within Analog Dance’s second album, Mind The Fall, that steamy pressure becomes one element in a larger design. Across eleven tracks and just under forty-five minutes, the London darkwave project turns collapse, concealment, desire, and performance into sensual dark electronic pop, with guitar supplying warmth or frost at carefully chosen moments. Mind The Fall, released July 22 through Poland’s Bat-Cave Productions, follows the project’s 2024 debut, Stranger Minds. Written and recorded in isolation in a wooden cabin in Argentina, the album carries the concentration that distance can bring. Its songs feel secluded and interior, while broad drum machines, elastic bass sequences, and clean guitar lines give them considerable physical force. The production is fuller and more exact than before, though the closeness of a private recording remains central to its appeal. In a 2024 interview, Jonny described Analog Dance as an alter ego created to express emotions that words alone could not carry. He also traced the project’s name to the tactile appeal of analog equipment and the ability of synthesizers to stir feeling and movement. Mind The Fall gives that idea its clearest form yet: the machines set bodies in motion, while his voice reveals the cost of maintaining control. The titles supply their own vocabulary. Wires and screens suggest mediation; masks and shows invoke presentation; decay, rot, and falling apart name what lies beneath. Even “A Clean Version of Hell” turns damage into something polished enough for display. These phrases create a thread across the record, and the music follows suit, pairing immaculate surfaces with uneasy motion underneath. “Ghost on a Wire” opens with low, fluttering synthesizers that carry a faintly occult charge, followed by a broad drum-machine strike and a simple rising-and-falling guitar figure. Jonny’s baritone enters deep, lush, and close, drawing the ear toward the center of the mix. The melody is economical enough to lodge after one pass, while the production gives every layer room to register. As an opener, it introduces the album’s governing attraction: machine precision warmed by a voice carrying unmistakable appetite. “A Clean Version of Hell” begins in metal and glass, patiently arranging hard-edged effects and cool high-register tones before a heavy ’80s drum pattern and rounded melodic bass take command. Crystalline guitar phrases hang above the rhythm as Jonny brings deep new-wave romance to the center. The title’s contradiction—hell sanitized, pain made presentable—anticipates the record’s later concern with screens, masks, and performance, while the music could easily accompany the most intimate scene in an unmade late-night thriller. “Fall Apart” gains additional meaning from its place in the sequence. The severe elegance remains: a rigid beat draws the room, the synthesizers constrict it, and unease passes from bass to percussion to the open space around the vocal. Its supple club gait occasionally recalls Boy Harsher’s more sensual turns, though Jonny’s elongated phrasing and the clean post-punk guitar keep the song firmly within Analog Dance’s own language. Positioned between “A Clean Version of Hell” and “Behind the Screen,” the lead single becomes the album’s hinge, connecting polished catastrophe to private longing. “Behind the Screen” fades in gradually, assembling drums, bell-like chimes, and broad, glassy pads in measured layers. The mood brings to mind a romantic scene from 2011’s Drive, with city light sliding across a windshield as a high guitar line curls upward through smoke. Jonny holds his notes longer here, allowing earnest tenderness to replace some of the album’s usual reserve. The result produces a quiet rush of serotonin, spacious and enveloping, with each element entering at precisely the right moment. “Five-Star Mask” starts with rippling synthesizers that recall S U R V I V E scoring one of Stranger Things’ dreamier passages. A single DX7-like digital preset flashes past—before the full dance beat settles in. Drums and bass carry the weight as a supple synthwave melody continues below Jonny’s low, sultry vocal. Glinting guitar and a buoyant ascending-and-descending motif complete an intimate midtempo dance, made for two people moving together while the surrounding room recedes. “Intimate Decay” lowers the temperature with wavering upper-register tones and a deep electronic hum, then suspends the arrangement for a breath before a rubbery bass sequence begins. Cold jolts repeat, the drums shudder, and a brief baroque figure rises and falls before Analog Dance’s favored high-register guitar enters. Jonny sustains his phrases above the accumulating layers until the texture feels nearly physical. The title’s pairing of closeness and decomposition could stand as the album’s thesis, and the track renders that friction with particular tenderness. “Same War Within” opens on gauzy pads, pinpoint synth notes, and a heavy kick before claps and a rippling bass line steer it toward Italo disco. Guitar serves as an accent at first, leaving generous space around the low vocal. A little over a minute in, the arrangement changes its balance: a burbling figure settles below the mix, the voice drops out, and the guitar takes melodic command before the two rejoin over a cool pad. That sequence of handoffs is among the album’s smartest structural moves, creating development through control rather than grandstanding. “Scenic Crime” eases the pace with subdued synthesizers, a measured drum pattern, and a bass backbone that keeps the song moving. A modest, immediately hummable keyboard melody appears, and the guitar soon traces its outline. The feeling is wistful, suspended somewhere between pleasure and loss, as Jonny’s smooth delivery settles over low melodic undertones and small electronic flourishes drift through the margins. Its emotional ambiguity gives the track its pull; the view is lovely, though something unresolved remains just beyond the frame. “Beautiful Rot” opens with distorted, icy electronics, then answers them with a rapid drum barrage and a muscular dance bass line, making this one of the record’s fastest selections. A buoyant sequence and clear bell tones prepare the entrance of Jonny’s baritone and a clean, chiming guitar, while his quicker vocal phrasing swoops around the percussion. The song turns the album’s central contradiction into movement, placing elegance and deterioration in the same body. Its speed and melodic abundance make it a late-record peak. “The Plastic Show” rides a cycling electronic sequence that remains in place while resonant chimes, low-register strings, and a cleaner guitar line accumulate around it. Jonny initially sounds more detached than he did on “Beautiful Rot,” but his delivery gathers pressure as the song proceeds. Frustration remains contained within the measured arrangement, creating the sense of somebody trying to keep up appearances while emotion presses against the surface. As the record’s clearest invocation of artificial display, it brings the album’s concern with performance into plain view. “Selling the Show” closes the album by fading into broad pads and skittering drums, immediately establishing a cinematic new-wave atmosphere. Metallic bass enters with a melodic bounce, the pace gathers, and Jonny’s voice guides the song through several cleanly placed breaks. Familiar burbling synthesizers and a luminous guitar line return, but the final vocal passages are compressed into a distant, radio-like signal. That treatment leaves the confession mediated and receding, as though private feeling has finally been packaged for transmission. Taken together, Mind The Fall draws openly from the memory of ’80s post-punk, darkwave, synthpop, synthwave, and film music, using those reference points as a working vocabulary. Analog Dance’s identity remains distinct: a low voice with considerable tenderness, forceful electronic drums, lucid guitar, and synthesizers that can suggest glass, smoke, metal, or silk. The album is sensual, emotionally exposed, and highly danceable, with pacing that gives desire and anxiety equal weight. Where Stranger Minds established the dimensions of Jonny’s private world, Mind The Fall brings its architecture into sharper focus. Recurring textures connect the songs, the titles deepen one another, and “Fall Apart” now reads as the center of an album preoccupied with the effort required to remain intact. It is Analog Dance’s most cohesive release so far, a record whose immaculate finish cannot conceal the strain moving underneath. Mind The Fall was released July 22 through Bat-Cave Productions and is available now on all streaming platforms. The physical CD edition can be ordered directly from the label, while the label’s Bandcamp offers a digital edition. Analog Dance credits Crimeframe for recording, production, mixing, and mastering, Rusty Pilgrim for artwork, and Synth Wizrd for design. Listen to Mind the Fall below or via Spotify and order it here. items.body:
The most perfectly formed Cocteau Twins album, perhaps one of the most perfectly formed albums of all time - soaked in bittersweet sorrow and nostalgia, it’s almost painful listening to it 30 years later.

Numerous publications have declared it one of the best albums of the 90s, with Pitchfork calling it “a core of ungodly gorgeous songs that is every bit as moving and relevant today as it ever was.”. Famously - 4AD founder Ivo Watts-Russell has called it his favourite all-time 4AD album, “by a long shot”. 

Recorded in the midst of much upheaval - the birth of Fraser and Guthrie's daughter, the death of Simon Raymonde’s father Ivor Raymonde, the disintegration of the band’s relationship with 4AD (this was to be their last album for the label) - the result is lucid and enveloping, you can even decipher some of Fraser’s lyrics on this one.

Anyway, Heaven or Las Vegas is really one of life’s great pleasures for anyone acquainted with it. And if you aren’t - get to it.

items._cn_summary: Cocteau Twins 的这张专辑诞生于乐队内部的动荡时期——成员经历了新生儿诞生、亲人离世以及与厂牌关系的终结，这些情感经历渗透进了音乐的肌理。Elizabeth Fraser 的声线在这张作品中相对清晰，部分歌词可以被辨认，这在乐队以往作品中并不常见。制作呈现出一种通透而包裹感强的质感，将酸涩的怀旧情绪与旋律的流动感交织在一起。Pitchfork 将其评为九十年代最佳专辑之一，4AD 创始人 Ivo Watts-Russell 也将其视为该厂牌历史上最杰出的作品。专辑在 shoegaze 音墙与氛围流行之间取得了平衡，既保留了乐队标志性的缥缈人声处理，又展现出更明确的情绪表达层次。
